report:
**Conclusion: The evidence does not support that coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) improves movement disorders in Parkinson's disease. Despite early promise, the best available clinical trial data show no significant benefit on motor symptoms.**

**Evidence:**

CoQ10, an antioxidant supporting mitochondrial function, showed neuroprotective potential in preclinical Parkinson's disease (PD) models, and an early phase II study suggested possible clinical benefit, raising hopes for a disease-modifying therapy. However, the definitive phase III randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled QE3 trial (the largest study, examining 1200 and 2400 mg/day in early PD patients) found **no evidence of benefit** in slowing functional decline or improving motor outcomes compared with placebo.

A 2016 meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (Zhu et al.) concluded that while CoQ10 was safe and well tolerated, it did **not** produce significant improvement in motor symptoms (as measured by the UPDRS motor score) or overall disability in PD patients. An earlier meta-analysis of eight RCTs (899 patients) similarly found no improvement of motor symptoms.

A 2022 systematic review (MDPI, Journal of Personalized Medicine) noted that although oxidative stress is implicated in PD pathogenesis and CoQ10 levels may be altered in patient tissues, clinical evidence for therapeutic efficacy in parkinsonian syndromes remains lacking.

An older Cochrane review suggested modest improvements in some secondary scores at 1200 mg/day for 16 months, but this finding was not replicated in subsequent larger trials and is outweighed by the more recent negative meta-analyses and the negative phase III QE3 trial.

**Sources:**
- https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/1851409
- https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10072-016-2757-9
- https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975
- https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/clinical-trials/effects-coenzyme-q10-coq-parkinson-disease
